Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil (CNN) -- Former presidents of Mexico, Colombia and Brazil called Wednesday for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use and a change in tactics on the war on drugs, a Spanish news agency said. People march in support of legalized marijuana in late January in Belem, northern Brazil. Ex-presidents Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, Cesar Gaviria of Colombia and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil made their announcement at a meeting in Brazil of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, the EFE news agency said. "The problem is that current policies are based on prejudices and fears and not on results," Gaviria said at a news conference in which the commission's recommendations were presented. The 17-member panel worked on the report for a year and will forward it to all Latin American governments as well as the United States and the European Union, EFE said. Gaviria said the time is right to start a debate on the subject, particularly with the pragmatic openings provided by the election of President Barack Obama in the United States. "In many states in the United States, as is the case in California, they have begun to change federal policies with regard to tolerating marijuana for therapeutic purposes. And in Washington there's some consensus that the current policy is failing," EFE quotes Gaviria as saying. Decriminalization should be accompanied by treatment for addicts and public service campaigns on abuse prevention, the commission said. "If you don't help those who are dependent, you are half way there because they are going to commit crime to get money and pay for the drug," Gaviria said. Cardoso said the group called for only the decriminalization of marijuana and not other illicit drugs because "you have to start somewhere" and it would have been unrealistic to ask the same for all drugs, EFE said. Marijuana was chosen because it is grown in all countries in the region and because it is "less harmful." The decades-old criminalization of personal consumption has failed to stop the plant's cultivation and distribution, the group said. The commission urged that all current criminal prosecution be aimed at drug cartels and organized crime and not marijuana smokers, EFE said. Zedillo did not attend the news conference but worked on the report, Cardoso said. Wednesday's recommendation was the second time in less than a week that a Latin American government official called for decriminalization. A mayor in Peru suggested Friday that the federal government legalize illicit drugs and administer them through the national health ministry. Gusto Sierra, the mayor of the Surquillo district in Lima, said a federal drug law is hypocritical because it allows maximum legally allowed quantities for some drugs and plants but doesn't say where to acquire them, the Peru 21 newspaper reported in a front-page story headlined "Say yes to drugs?" Sierra said he will take the matter up with the nation's executive branch. Zedillo served as president of Mexico from 1994-2000. Gaviria was president of Colombia from 1990-94. And Cardoso led Brazil from 1995-2002.

### Option 1: Refined Journalistic Style (Recommended)

**RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil (CNN)** — Former presidents of Mexico, Colombia, and Brazil convened on Wednesday to advocate for a fundamental shift in drug policy, calling for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal consumption and a strategic overhaul of the global "war on drugs," according to the Spanish news agency EFE. 

The announcement coincides with growing regional momentum, underscored by a late-January demonstration in Belém, northern Brazil, where citizens marched in support of marijuana legalization. 

Speaking on behalf of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy during a conference in Brazil, former presidents Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, César Gaviria of Colombia, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil presented the panel’s newly unveiled recommendations. 

"The fundamental flaw is that existing policies are rooted in prejudice and apprehension rather than empirical results," Gaviria stated during the press conference. 

The 17-member commission spent a year formulating the report, which will be formally submitted to governments across Latin America, as well as to the United States and the European Union. Gaviria emphasized that the current political climate presents an ideal moment to initiate this dialogue, citing pragmatic shifts under the administration of U.S. President Barack Obama. 

"Across several U.S. states, most notably California, federal policy is beginning to evolve toward greater tolerance of therapeutic marijuana use. Furthermore, there is a growing consensus in Washington that current strategy is failing," Gaviria noted.

The commission emphasized that decriminalization must be paired with comprehensive rehabilitation programs for substance dependency and public education campaigns aimed at abuse prevention. "Failing to assist those struggling with addiction addresses only half the problem, as individuals will inevitably turn to crime to finance their habit," Gaviria warned.

Addressing why the proposal focuses exclusively on marijuana, Cardoso explained that "one must begin somewhere," acknowledging that demanding the immediate decriminalization of all illicit substances would be unrealistic. Marijuana was selected due to its regional ubiquity and significantly lower harm profile compared to other drugs. Decades of criminalizing personal possession have failed to curb the plant's cultivation or distribution, the panel concluded. Consequently, the commission urged law enforcement authorities to redirect their resources away from individual users and concentrate exclusively on drug cartels and organized crime.

While former Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo was unable to attend the press conference, Cardoso confirmed that he actively contributed to the report. 

Wednesday’s announcement marks the second time in less than a week that a Latin American official has called for drug policy reform. On Friday, Mayor Gusto Sierra of Lima's Surquillo district urged Peru's federal government to legalize illicit substances and manage their distribution through the national health ministry. 

Reporting on the proposal in a front-page article titled *"Say yes to drugs?"*, the newspaper *Peru 21* quoted Sierra as calling federal drug laws hypocritical for permitting maximum legal possession limits without providing lawful means of acquisition. Sierra indicated plans to raise the matter directly with the nation's executive branch.

The three statesmen leading the commission carry significant regional authority: Gaviria served as president of Colombia from 1990 to 1994; Zedillo led Mexico from 1994 to 2000; and Cardoso governed Brazil from 1995 to 2002.

**Headline:** Rethinking the War on Drugs: Latin American Commission Calls for Marijuana Decriminalization and Health-Centered Reform

For decades, the global "war on drugs" has been waged primarily through strict prohibition, military enforcement, and criminal prosecution. However, a growing consensus among policy experts suggests that these traditional approaches have failed to curb consumption or reduce violence, relying instead on political dogma and deeply ingrained moral prejudices. In response to this ongoing crisis, a high-level panel of 17 distinguished members—including former Latin American presidents, prominent intellectuals, and public health experts—spent a year conducting an exhaustive evaluation of regional drug policies on behalf of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy.

The panel’s long-awaited report presents a stark assessment: current prohibitionist strategies have proven inefficient, costly, and counterproductive. By focusing resources on penalizing consumers and low-level offenders, governments have strained judicial systems and overcrowded prisons without weakening the power of transnational organized crime. To break this destructive cycle, the Commission’s report offers a comprehensive roadmap intended for presentation to both regional governments and the broader international community, advocating for a pragmatic shift toward evidence-based public policy.

At the heart of the Commission’s recommendations is a call to decriminalize the possession and use of marijuana for personal consumption. Rather than treating substance use as a criminal matter, the report urges governments to reallocate law enforcement resources toward tackling violent drug-trafficking networks. Simultaneously, the state should treat drug use primarily as a public health issue, investing heavily in robust addiction treatment programs, harm reduction initiatives, and targeted public prevention campaigns. 

The panel identified the decriminalization of cannabis as the most realistic and strategic starting point for broader drug policy reform. This conclusion is rooted in two pragmatic realities: first, scientific evidence consistently demonstrates that marijuana carries a significantly lower risk of harm and dependency compared to illicit hard drugs or even legally available substances like alcohol and tobacco. Second, cannabis is cultivated extensively throughout Latin America, making total eradication nearly impossible and enforcement efforts endlessly expensive. 

By starting with cannabis, the Commission argues, nations can build a sensible, phased alternative to prohibition that protects civil liberties, reduces social harm, and prioritizes human health. The report serves as a bold call to action, challenging regional and international leaders to abandon outdated, prejudice-driven mandates in favor of a rational policy framework that yields real, measurable results.

Nestled between lush tropical mountains and the deep blue expanse of the Atlantic Ocean lies one of the most mesmerizing urban landscapes on Earth. Welcome to **Rio** de **Janeiro**, the beating heart of **Brazil**’s cultural identity. Affectionately known as the *"Cidade Maravilhosa"* (The Marvelous City), Rio is a place where dramatic natural beauty and electric human energy merge into an unforgettable experience.

Standing high above the city, the iconic Christ the Redeemer statue atop Corcovado Mountain opens its arms to welcome millions of visitors each year, offering a peaceful contrast to the lively metropolis below. Nearby, the granite peak of Sugarloaf Mountain rises from Guanabara Bay, providing panoramic views of a city sculpted by nature. 

Yet, the true soul of Rio de Janeiro is found at sea level. The legendary golden sands of Copacabana and Ipanema are more than just beaches—they are vibrant social arenas. Here, locals (known as *Cariocas*) gather to play footvolley, sip cold coconut water, and celebrate the outdoor lifestyle that makes Brazil famous worldwide.

Beyond its postcard-worthy views, Rio is powered by an undeniable rhythm. It is the birthplace of samba and bossa nova, soundscapes that reflect both the joyful energy and the poetic melancholy of Brazilian life. This passion reaches its peak during Carnival, the world’s greatest street party, when the city transforms into an explosion of color, elaborate costumes, and non-stop dancing led by the samba schools in the Sambadrome.

From the bohemian streets of Santa Teresa and the lively nightlife of Lapa to the serene expanse of the Tijuca National Forest, Rio de Janeiro is a city of captivating contrasts. It is a destination that doesn't just show you its beauty—it invites you to feel its warmth, dance to its pulse, and fall in love with the irreplaceable spirit of Brazil.

The unprecedented recommendation comes from the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, a body convened to evaluate the social, political, and security impacts of illicit drug trafficking in the region. 

The commission is co-chaired by three former heads of state who once stood on the front lines of the drug war: Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil, Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, and César Gaviria of Colombia.

In a sweeping report, the leaders argue that military-style prohibition and mass incarceration have failed to curb consumption or disrupt organized crime, while placing an intolerable strain on Latin America’s democratic institutions, judicial systems, and public safety.

"The war on drugs has failed," former Colombian President César Gaviria said during the presentation of the commission’s findings. "The prohibitionist policy based on eradication, interdiction, and criminalization has not yielded the expected results. Today, we are further away from eradicating drugs than we were 30 years ago."

Gaviria, who led Colombia during the bloody combat against Pablo Escobar’s Medellín cartel in the early 1990s, emphasized that a fresh approach is urgently needed to break the cycle of violence that plagues the region.

"We must break the taboo," Gaviria added. "Treating consumers as criminals only overburdens our legal systems and prevents us from addressing drug use for what it truly is—a public health issue."

### A Shift Toward Public Health

The commission's primary proposal centers on decriminalizing cannabis for personal consumption, shifting state resources from arresting low-level users toward prevention, treatment, and harm reduction. 

By removing small-scale possession from the criminal justice system, the leaders argue, police and judicial authorities can redirect crucial resources toward combating violent transnational cartels, money laundering, and heavy weapons trafficking.

The report also emphasizes that decriminalization does not mean surrender. Instead, it advocates for a regulated legal framework that deprives violent criminal syndicates of one of their primary revenue streams.

### Regional Momentum Building

The commission's recommendations reflect a growing appetite for drug policy reform across South and Central America, where local leaders are increasingly experimenting with alternative approaches.

In Peru, where cocoa and cannabis trafficking remain persistent challenges, the mayor of a major district in Lima recently raised eyebrows by proposing the legalization and state regulation of marijuana. The mayor argued that local law enforcement is overwhelmed by low-level drug offenses, and that regulating personal use would immediately reduce street-level crime and free up officers to fight violent gang activity.

Similar debates are surfacing across Latin America, as current and former officials recognize that traditional enforcement strategies—heavily backed for decades by U.S. counter-narcotics funding—have done little to reduce overall global supply.

While the commission's proposal is expected to face resistance from conservative lawmakers and international drug enforcement agencies, the former presidents insist that maintaining the status quo is no longer viable.

"We cannot continue repeating the same mistakes and expecting different results," Gaviria said. "It is time for Latin America to lead a rational, human-rights-based dialogue on the future of drug policy."

**Yes, this historic event did happen.** In February 2009, a high-profile group of former Latin American leaders united under the **Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy** to declare the U.S.-led "War on Drugs" a failure and advocate for the decriminalization of marijuana. 

Below is a news report detailing their landmark meeting in Rio de Janeiro and their recommendations.

***

# Latin American Leaders Declare 'War on Drugs' a Failure, Call for Marijuana Decriminalization at Rio Summit

**RIO DE JANEIRO** — In a historic shift in regional policy discourse, a commission of prominent former Latin American presidents met in Rio de Janeiro to declare that the decades-long, prohibitionist "War on Drugs" has failed. The leaders jointly advocated for a dramatic policy overhaul, recommending the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use and a pivot toward viewing drug consumption as a public health issue rather than a criminal one.

The initiative was spearheaded by the **Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy**, co-chaired by three former heads of state who presided over nations heavily impacted by drug trafficking and cartels:
* **Fernando Henrique Cardoso**, former President of Brazil
* **César Gaviria**, former President of Colombia
* **Ernesto Zedillo**, former President of Mexico

The commission, which also included 14 other prominent intellectuals, journalists, and public figures—such as Peruvian Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa—presented a comprehensive report titled *"Drugs and Democracy: Towards a Paradigm Shift."*

### A Failed Strategy and a High Price

Speaking at a press conference in Rio de Janeiro, the former leaders argued that current prohibition policies have neither curbed global drug consumption nor stopped the illegal drug trade. Instead, they argued, Latin America has paid a devastating price in blood, corruption, and political instability.

"The prohibitionist strategy based on repression of production and interdiction of traffic has not produced the expected results," said former Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso. "We are further than ever from the goal of eradicating drugs. The current policy is simply not working."

Former Colombian President César Gaviria, who led his nation during the height of the violent war against Pablo Escobar’s Medellín cartel in the early 1990s, emphasized the urgent need to break the political taboo surrounding drug policy. "We must break the silence," Gaviria urged. "Latin America remains the region most affected by violence and criminality linked to the drug trade, yet the current policies are failing our people."

### Key Recommendations

The commission laid out three main pillars for a new, regional drug strategy:

1. **Decriminalize Personal Marijuana Consumption:** The report explicitly recommended that governments cease treating drug users as criminals. It singled out marijuana, noting that it accounts for the vast majority of illegal drug use, and urged states to decriminalize possession for personal use.
2. **Treat Addiction as a Public Health Issue:** The leaders called for a massive reallocation of state resources away from prisons and law enforcement and toward public education, harm reduction programs, and addiction treatment. 
3. **Refocus Law Enforcement on Violence:** Rather than targeting small-scale consumers or low-level farmers (cocaleros), security forces should focus exclusively on dismantling organized crime networks, human trafficking, illegal arms flows, and violent cartels that pose a direct threat to democratic governance.

### A Watershed Moment

The Rio meeting marked the first time that a organized group of former Latin American heads of state publicly united to challenge the prevailing international drug control paradigm, long championed by the United States. 

While active politicians in the region historically avoided the topic for fear of political backlash or U.S. sanctions, the status of these leaders as elder statesmen allowed them to speak candidly about the failures of prohibition.

The commission’s declaration in Rio de Janeiro laid the groundwork for future global debates. (It eventually evolved into the Global Commission on Drug Policy in 2011) and influenced individual national policies, including Uruguay’s landmark decision years later to become the first country in the world to fully legalize and regulate the cannabis market.

The leaders concluded their summit by urging current Latin American heads of state to take up the mantle, break the taboo, and push for a rational, science-based approach to international drug policy.

**Title:** From the Frontlines to the Forefront: How Former Latin American Presidents Challenged the War on Drugs

For decades, Latin America served as the primary battleground for the global "War on Drugs." Heavy militarization, eradication of crops, and strict penal codes were the standard playbook, largely urged and funded by international policy. Yet, the flow of narcotics continued, cartel violence escalated, and prisons overflowed. 

Recognizing that the status quo was causing more damage than the drugs themselves, an unexpected coalition emerged in the late 2000s. A group of former Latin American presidents—most notably Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil, César Gaviria of Colombia, and Ernesto Zedillo (later joined by Vicente Fox) of Mexico—did something rare in politics: they publicly admitted that the policies they once enforced had failed, and they called for a fundamental paradigm shift toward the legalization and regulation of personal marijuana use.

### The Turning Point: The 2009 Commission

The watershed moment came in 2009 with the formation of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, co-chaired by Cardoso, Gaviria, and Zedillo. Shortly after, this initiative expanded globally into the **Global Commission on Drug Policy**. 

Their thesis was bold and unprecedented for high-level statesmen from the region: **The War on Drugs had been a catastrophic failure.** 

In a landmark declaration, the commission urged governments to break the taboo surrounding drug policy and shift from a law-enforcement model to one based on public health, human rights, and harm reduction. At the center of their recommendations was the decriminalization and legal regulation of cannabis for personal use.

### The Leaders and Their Lessons

The advocacy of these former leaders carried immense weight because each had presided over nations devastated by the drug trade.

*   **Fernando Henrique Cardoso (Brazil, President 1995–2002):** 
    As the chair of the commission, Cardoso focused heavily on the social cost of prohibition. In Brazil, zero-tolerance policies led to mass incarceration, predominantly affecting poor and minority youth caught with small amounts of cannabis, while doing little to dismantle powerful prison gangs. Cardoso argued that treating cannabis as a public health issue would free up police resources to fight violent crime and reduce the stigmatization of users.

*   **César Gaviria (Colombia, President 1990–1994):** 
    Gaviria led Colombia during one of its violent eras, overseeing the hunt for cartel kingpin Pablo Escobar. Having seen firsthand the appalling human cost of supply-side eradication, Gaviria argued that as long as consumer demand in wealthy nations remained high, Latin America would continue to bleed. He advocated that legalizing personal marijuana use was a necessary first step to strip criminal syndicates of their primary source of revenue and reduce the systemic violence plagueing consumer and transit nations alike.

*   **Ernesto Zedillo (Mexico, President 1994–2000) and Vicente Fox (President 2000–2006):** 
    Zedillo co-authored early reports advocating for a shift away from criminalization, acknowledging that Mexico’s security apparatus was being eroded by cartel wealth. His successor, Vicente Fox, became perhaps the most vocal post-presidential advocate for cannabis legalization in the Americas. Fox argued that prohibition was an archaic restriction on individual liberty and economic potential, asserting that legalizing and taxing marijuana would transform a bloody black market into a legitimate, job-creating industry.

### The Core Recommendations

The former leaders outlined a clear blueprint for reform, urging governments to abandon ideological rigidity in favor of pragmatic policy:

1.  **Decriminalize Personal Possession:** Treat the possession of small amounts of cannabis for personal use as an administrative or health matter, not a criminal offense.
2.  **Focus Law Enforcement on Violent Crime:** Redirect police, judicial, and military resources away from casual cannabis users and small-time growers, focusing instead on organized crime, human trafficking, and violence.
3.  **Establish Legal Regulatory Frameworks:** Shift control of the cannabis market from cartels to the state through taxation, age limits, quality controls, and public education—similar to the regulation of alcohol and tobacco.
4.  **Prioritize Public Health and Harm Reduction:** Reallocate funds previously spent on incarceration toward voluntary drug treatment, prevention programs, and medical research.

### A Domino Effect Across the Americas

When these leaders first made their recommendations, their views were considered radical. However, their political stature provided "cover" for sitting politicians and jurists to reconsider their approach to drug reform. 

The ripples of their advocacy transformed policy across the Western Hemisphere:

*   In **2013, Uruguay** became the first country in the world to fully legalize and regulate the adult use of cannabis.
*   In **Mexico**, a series of Supreme Court rulings declared the prohibition of personal cannabis use unconstitutional, prompting ongoing legislative efforts to formalize a legal market.
*   In **Brazil**, the Supreme Court ruled in 2024 to decriminalize the possession of marijuana for personal use, establishing clear quantitative thresholds to distinguish users from traffickers.
*   The movement also influenced policy in North America, contributing to full legalization in Canada and across dozens of U.S. states.

### Conclusion

The intervention of Cardoso, Gaviria, Zedillo, and Fox marked a critical turning point in global drug policy. By leveraging their post-presidential authority, they reframed cannabis prohibition not as a necessary moral crusade, but as a costly, ineffective policy that fueled violence and weakened democratic institutions. 

Their message remains relevant today: policy should be judged by its results, not its intentions. By advocating for legal regulation and public health over prohibition and incarceration, these former leaders helped chart a pragmatic path forward for the Americas.

**POLICY & POLITICS**

# 'The War on Drugs Has Failed': How a Landmark Latin American Report Changed the Global Cannabis Debate

**By News Desk**  
*Published 8:00 AM EST*

In a move that fundamentally reshaped international drug policy, a heavyweight panel of former Latin American presidents and public intellectuals delivered a stark verdict that reverberated around the world: the decades-long, U.S.-led "War on Drugs" was a catastrophic failure, and it was time to decriminalize marijuana.

The Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy—co-chaired by former presidents Fernando Henrique Cardoso (Brazil), César Gaviria (Colombia), and Ernesto Zedillo (Mexico)—shattered a long-standing political taboo with its landmark report, *Drugs and Democracy: Toward a Paradigm Shift*. 

By advocating for a shift away from law enforcement and toward public health, the commission touched off a global media storm and laid the groundwork for the modern cannabis reform movement across the Americas.

---

### The Key Findings: A Broken Strategy and a New Path Forward

The commission’s report was grounded in a harsh reality: despite billions of dollars spent on eradication, interdiction, and militarized police responses, drug consumption and violent crime had continued to rise across Latin America.

The key takeaways from the report included:

* **Prohibition Has Failed:** The strategy of total prohibition and criminalization failed to reduce production or consumption. Instead, it empowered organized crime, corrupted democratic institutions, and fueled unprecedented levels of violence.
* **Decriminalize Marijuana for Personal Use:** The panel urged governments to treat cannabis consumers not as criminals, but as a public health concern. Decriminalizing personal possession, the report argued, would reduce court backlogs, empty overcrowded prisons, and break the link between casual users and illicit cartels.
* **Focus on High-Value Targets:** Rather than arresting low-level users and small-scale farmers, police and military resources should be redirected toward dismantling violent trafficking syndicates, money laundering operations, and arms smugglers.
* **Prioritize Public Health and Harm Reduction:** The report called for significantly higher investment in drug education, addiction treatment, and harm-reduction strategies, framing substance abuse as a medical issue rather than a moral or legal failure.

---

### Heavyweight Leaders Break the Taboo

What made the report a bombshell was not just its content, but its authors. 

Cardoso, Gaviria, and Zedillo were not radical activists; they were elder statesmen who had governed countries on the frontlines of the drug war. Gaviria, in particular, had led Colombia during its bloodiest battles against Pablo Escobar's Medellín cartel in the 1990s. Joining them were prominent Latin American writers and intellectuals, including Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa.

"To break the taboo and acknowledge that the current policy has failed is a necessary first step," President Cardoso said during the report's release, noting that Latin America could no longer afford to pay the highest price in human lives for a strategy that wasn't working.

---

### Global News Coverage: A "Seismic Shift" in Public Discourse

The release of the report generated widespread international media coverage, with major outlets framing it as a turning point in international relations and domestic policy.

* **The New York Times** highlighted that the report represented "the most high-profile challenge yet" to U.S.-sponsored drug policies in the Western Hemisphere, noting that Latin American leaders were tired of bearing the brunt of American drug consumption.
* **The BBC** emphasized the human cost detailed in the report, reporting that prohibition had severely undermined Latin America's democratic institutions and created an unsustainable crisis in the region's judicial systems.
* **El País** and regional Latin American media hailed the document for breaking decades of silence, calling it a long-overdue act of political realism that reflected the growing frustration of regional governments.

---

### The Aftermath and Lasting Legacy

The initial reaction from Western governments was cautious, if not resistant. At the time, the U.S. Office of National Drug Control Policy pushed back against the commission's recommendations, reiterating the Obama administration's opposition to legalizing or decriminalizing drugs. Conservative political sectors across Latin America also expressed concern that decriminalization might lead to increased addiction rates.

However, the report's long-term impact proved unstoppable. 

The commission’s work acted as a catalyst, giving political cover to current heads of state to question the status quo. Just a few years later, in 2013, Uruguay became the first country in the world to fully legalize and regulate adult-use cannabis. Mexico’s Supreme Court would later rule cannabis prohibition unconstitutional, and Colombia dramatically reformed its personal possession laws.

Furthermore, the Latin American Commission served as the blueprint for the **Global Commission on Drug Policy**, which expanded the push for reform globally, attracting figures like former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan and Sir Richard Branson to the cause.

More than a decade after its release, the Latin American Commission’s report is remembered as the opening salvo in a global shift—transforming marijuana decriminalization from a fringe proposal into a mainstream policy tool for human rights, public health, and security reform.
